title: Question 2
stem:
An object of constant mass moves in a straight line. The variation with time $t$ of the momentum $p$ of the object is shown in Fig. 2.1.

{{figure:figure_2_1}}

parts.label: (a)
hints: Hint 1: Think about which two properties of a moving object combine to tell you how hard it is to stop it - one related to how much matter it has and one related to its motion.
parts.proper_answer: Momentum is the product of mass and velocity.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **What Momentum Means**
Think of momentum as the quantity of motion an object has. A heavy lorry moving slowly and a light bullet moving very fast can both be hard to stop because both have large momentum.

Step 2: **Exact Definition**
For an object of mass $m$ moving with velocity $v$, momentum $p$ is defined by $$p = mv$$ So in words, momentum is the product of mass and velocity.

parts.label: (b)
parts.text: Calculate the change in momentum of the object from time $t = 0$ to $t = 12\text{ s}$.

markscheme_points.text: change in momentum = (-1.4) - (+2.8) = (-) 4.2 kg m s^-1

hints: Hint 1: Read the starting value of $p$ at $t = 0$ and the finishing value of $p$ at $t = 12\text{ s}$ from Fig. 2.1, taking careful note of the sign when the line goes below zero.
parts.proper_answer: $\Delta p = -1.4 - (+2.8) = -4.2\text{ kg m s}^{-1}$, so change is $4.2\text{ kg m s}^{-1}$ in the negative direction.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Final Minus Initial**
Change always means final value minus initial value. From Fig. 2.1, at $t = 0$, $$p_i = +2.8\text{ kg m s}^{-1}$$ and at $t = 12\text{ s}$, $$p_f = -1.4\text{ kg m s}^{-1}$$

Step 2: **Subtract With Signs**
$$\Delta p = p_f - p_i = (-1.4) - (+2.8) = -4.2\text{ kg m s}^{-1}$$ The negative sign shows momentum has decreased and reversed direction.

parts.label: (c)
parts.text: Calculate the magnitude of the resultant force acting on the object.
hints: Hint 1: Look at the shape of Fig. 2.1 - it is a straight line. Think about what the steepness or gradient of a momentum-time graph tells you in physics.
Hint 2: Use the change in momentum from (b) over the 12 s time interval to find the rate of change, remembering magnitude means you give a positive value.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Force Is The Gradient**
Newton's second law can be written as force equals rate of change of momentum: $$F = \frac{\Delta p}{\Delta t}$$ On a $p$ against $t$ graph this is the magnitude of the gradient. Because Fig. 2.1 is straight, the force is constant.

Step 2: **Put In The Numbers**
Magnitude of change is $4.2\text{ kg m s}^{-1}$ over $\Delta t = 12\text{ s}$: $$F = \frac{4.2}{12} = 0.35\text{ N}$$

parts.label: (d)
parts.text: Describe the variation of the speed of the object from time $t = 0$ to $t = 8.0\text{ s}$.

markscheme_points.text: constant / uniform (rate of) decrease (of speed to zero).

hints: Hint 1: Remember mass is constant, so speed follows the size of $p$ ignoring its sign. Look at how the height of the line above the $t$-axis changes from $t = 0$ to where it hits zero at $t = 8.0\text{ s}$.
parts.proper_answer: Speed decreases uniformly (at a constant rate) from its initial value to zero at $t = 8.0\text{ s}$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Link Speed To Momentum**
With constant mass, $v = p/m$, so speed is proportional to the magnitude of $p$. From $t = 0$ to $t = 8.0\text{ s}$, $p$ falls on a straight line from $2.8\text{ kg m s}^{-1}$ to zero.

Step 2: **Describe The Motion**
A straight $p$-$t$ graph means a constant rate of change. So the speed shows a constant or uniform decrease to zero at $8.0\text{ s}$. Speed has no direction, so we just say it falls to zero.

parts.label: (e)
parts.text: By reference to Fig. 2.1, explain why the resultant force acting on the object during the first $8.0\text{ s}$ of its motion cannot be due to air resistance.

markscheme_points.text: • The (resultant) force is constant / does not decrease • air resistance would vary / decrease / not constant • the force is not zero when speed / velocity is zero / at 8 s
markscheme_points.guidance: Any two of the above 3 marking points (1 mark each, max 2)

hints: Hint 1: Compare what Fig. 2.1 tells you about the resultant force - is its size changing or staying the same while the object slows down?
Hint 2: Think about how air resistance or drag normally behaves - what should happen to it as speed drops toward zero, and what does the graph show is still happening at $t = 8.0\text{ s}$?
parts.proper_answer: The gradient of Fig. 2.1 is constant so the resultant force is constant. Air resistance would decrease as speed decreases and would be zero when speed is zero at 8.0 s, but a non-zero force is still acting. Hence it cannot be air resistance.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **What The Graph Shows**
Fig. 2.1 is a straight line, so its gradient $\Delta p / \Delta t$ is constant. That means the resultant force is constant in size and direction during the first $8.0\text{ s}$.

Step 2: **What Air Resistance Would Do**
Air resistance depends on speed. As the object slows down from $t = 0$ to $t = 8.0\text{ s}$, drag should get smaller and become zero when speed is zero at $8.0\text{ s}$.

Step 3: **Spot The Contradiction**
The graph shows the same steep slope, so the same force, even at $8.0\text{ s}$ when $p = 0$ and $v = 0$. A constant force that is still non-zero at zero speed cannot be air resistance alone.

parts.label: (f)
parts.text:
At time $t = 0$ the displacement $d$ of the object is zero.

On Fig. 2.2, sketch the variation of $d$ with time $t$ from $t = 0$ to $t = 12\text{ s}$.

Numerical values of $d$ are not required.

{{figure:figure_2_2}}

markscheme_points.text: line from origin with decreasing positive gradient
gradient changes from positive to negative at 8.0 s
after t = 8.0 s the line has a negative gradient of increasing magnitude and a positive value of d at t = 12 s

hints: Hint 1: Start at the origin and think about velocity - it is positive but getting smaller to zero at $t = 8.0\text{ s}$, so what should happen to the steepness of a $d$-$t$ graph?
Hint 2: At $t = 8.0\text{ s}$ the object momentarily stops. What does that mean for the $d$-$t$ graph - does $d$ keep rising, flatten, or fall?
Hint 3: After $t = 8.0\text{ s}$ momentum is negative and growing in size, so the object moves back. Think about the sign of the $d$-$t$ slope and whether $d$ at $t = 12\text{ s}$ is still positive.
parts.proper_answer: Curve starting at origin with decreasing positive gradient, flattening to zero gradient at $t = 8.0\text{ s}$, then with negative gradient of increasing magnitude, remaining at positive $d$ at $t = 12\text{ s}$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **First Part - Slowing Down Forwards**
Velocity is the gradient of a displacement-time graph. From $t = 0$ to $8.0\text{ s}$ velocity is positive but decreasing uniformly to zero. So start at $(0,0)$ and draw a curve with a decreasing positive gradient - getting flatter and flatter.

Step 2: **The Top Of The Curve**
At $t = 8.0\text{ s}$, $p = 0$ so $v = 0$. The object instantaneously stops at its maximum displacement. Your $d$-$t$ curve must have zero gradient there, like the top of a hill.

Step 3: **Coming Back**
After $8.0\text{ s}$, $p$ is negative and its magnitude grows, so velocity is negative and speed increases. The $d$-$t$ gradient becomes negative and gets steeper. Displacement falls but in only $4.0\text{ s}$ of return it cannot get back to zero, so at $t = 12\text{ s}$ $d$ is still positive.
